planting.note: Scatter seed on bare, lean sand in spring and press in lightly rather than burying it, since this scrub native germinates best with light exposure and sharp drainage.

directions: Sow directly into deep, infertile, excessively drained sand in full sun and avoid fertilizer or supplemental watering once seedlings are up. This upright, silvery-woolly scrub native carries dense, felted spikes of tiny white flowers from summer through fall above narrow gray-green leaves, giving it a soft, cottony texture unlike almost anything else in a xeric planting. It self-sows readily in open sandy gaps and persists best where competing vegetation stays sparse, making it a good filler for restoration plantings or a dry, open rock-garden-style bed. Cut back spent flower stalks in winter to tidy the clump and encourage fresh basal growth the following spring.
sources: Atlas of Florida Plants (University of South Florida)

planting.note: Sow seed in fall into lean, deep, well-drained sand in full sun; a cool, moist stratification period over winter improves spring emergence of this sandhill-scrub native.

directions: Plant in deep, dry, infertile sand in full sun, the same lean conditions it occupies naturally on sand pine scrub and sandhill margins across the Southeast. A basal rosette of felted, woolly gray-green leaves sends up branching, white-woolly flower stalks in late summer and fall, topped with small clusters of pale pink-to-white flowers that are an important late-season nectar source for native bees and migrating monarchs. It is intolerant of rich soil, mulch, or irrigation beyond establishment, which cause weak, floppy growth and rot. Leave the dried flower stalks standing into winter for seed-dispersal and habitat value, then cut back in late winter before new growth resumes.

planting.note: Nick or lightly sand the hard seed coat and sow in fall directly into deep, loose, well-drained sand in full sun; like most lupines it resents root disturbance, so avoid transplanting seedlings.

directions: Direct sow scarified seed into deep, loose, excessively drained sand in full sun, mimicking the open dunes and sand pine scrub of the Florida Panhandle Gulf coast where this species occurs naturally. Silvery, hairy palmate leaves form a loose clump that sends up spikes of fragrant violet-blue, pea-like flowers in late winter and early spring, well before most other scrub wildflowers bloom. It is a true short-lived perennial that performs best where sand stays loose and unamended, and it does not tolerate heavy soil, standing water, or competition from turf or mulch. Allow some pods to ripen and shatter in place each year to maintain a self-sustaining colony, since nursery-grown plants are often short-lived individually.
sources: Atlas of Florida Plants (University of South Florida)

planting.note: Direct sow onto lean, sandy soil in full sun to light shade in spring; this Florida endemic self-sows readily once a few plants are established in open sand.

directions: Grow in lean, sandy, well-drained soil in full sun to light shade along the margins of scrub and sandhill where it occurs naturally in peninsular Florida. This erect, unbranched endemic wildflower bears a dense, candle-like spike of small white-to-pink flowers at its tip for much of the warm season, a distinctive silhouette that gives it strong garden presence despite its slender habit. It is short-lived but reseeds freely in open, disturbed sand, so leave some spent spikes in place to maintain a naturalized patch. Avoid rich soil, heavy mulch, and dense groundcover, all of which outcompete its seedlings.
sources: Atlas of Florida Plants (University of South Florida)

planting.note: Set container-grown divisions or seedlings in spring into lean, sandy, well-drained soil in full sun; this slow-growing Florida endemic is almost always planted from nursery stock rather than direct-sown seed.

directions: Plant in lean, well-drained sandy soil in full sun, where this clump-forming grass-like perennial tolerates the periodic fire and seasonal drought of its native scrub and sandhill margins. Narrow, arching, blue-green evergreen leaves form a dense basal tuft that stays attractive year-round, and mature clumps send up tall, branched flower stalks studded with tiny cream flowers in late spring to summer. It is state-listed as threatened in Florida because of habitat loss, so source plants only from nurseries propagating from cultivated stock rather than wild-collected material. Established clumps need essentially no irrigation or fertilizer and resent heavy, poorly drained soils.
sources: Atlas of Florida Plants (University of South Florida)
